body.text: On Danny Rahamim's forearm, a new tattoo provides a solemn reminder of what his community lost three years ago, and what he believed it needed to protect its future.
He picked a sunflower because it always turns towards the light, along with the phrase "the way to hope".
"I divide [the people of Israel as those] who lost their hope, [and] people who keep the hope," Mr Rahamim told the ABC.
"I'm on the side that keeps the hope. Why? Because if you lost your hope, nothing will change."
On the sunflower's stem is the date that changed his family and country forever — October 7, 2023.
Three years on from the Hamas-led attacks on Israel, which killed around 1,200 people and resulted in 251 being taken hostage, Mr Rahamim insists hope was often in short supply.
"One day [there will be] peace, I have no doubt," he said.
"Maybe it won't happen in my lifetime, but as I told you, I have the responsibility to give the hope for my children and my grandchildren."
And as his country prepared for an election on October 27, Mr Rahamim argued a change of government was the only way to ensure that.
"This government is the most terrible and bad government that we ever had," he said.
"[If they] take the power in the next election, I think that Israel is in a very, very bad situation."
Will life ever return to normal?
Mr Rahamim has lived in Nahal Oz since 1975, a kibbutz roughly 800 metres away from the Gaza fence line.

Mr Rahamim said three waves of Hamas terrorists alongside several other armed groups poured over the Gaza fence line on October 7 and attacked Nahal Oz, as they did other communities along what is known as the Gaza Envelope.
Fifteen people were killed in the kibbutz, eight were taken hostage. Mr Rahamim and his family survived.
"I don't know how we survived. Just 30 metres behind our house … they went inside [a] house, shot the door of the safe room, the bullets came through the door and killed [a woman]," he said.
"It was like Russian roulette."
Around 85 per cent of the roughly 450 people who lived in Nahal Oz before the Hamas attacks have returned.
Sitting under a tree in the centre of the kibbutz, an Israeli surveillance drone buzzes overhead — keeping a close eye on the situation just over the border.
The proximity of the Israeli military holding territory inside Gaza helps Mr Rahamim's family feel safe being back in Nahal Oz.
He wants the army to stay there, to make sure Hamas does not return.
"I still believe that we have to make peace with the Palestinians, but not with the Hamas.
Mr Rahamim is a self-professed peace activist, and no fan of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Reports suggesting Mr Netanyahu was warned of a looming attack by Hamas and that he failed to pass on the intelligence has been a bitter pill to swallow.
"We are very, very angry. You hear it from 90 per cent of the population here," Mr Rahamim said.
"But unfortunately, if you go to Sderot, they will tell you that [Mr Netanyahu] saved Israel."
Mr Netanyahu has roundly rejected the reports, and launched legal action against the media outlets which published the accusations
Looking over to Gaza
In nearby Sderot, which was also overrun by Hamas on October 7, a lookout on the city's edge provides a view over the fence line and into northern Gaza.
In the distance is the rubble of what were once communities such as Beit Hanoun and Jabalia.
Much of the territory has been razed to the ground, as Israel targets what it says have been Hamas fighters and facilities.
More than 74,000 Palestinians, many of them civilians, have been killed in the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run Ministry of Health.
Caryn Oberman was among those at the lookout, which was built after October 7 and has attracted tourists, school groups and residents who can watch Israel's war in Gaza from the perimeter.
Her daughter was living in Sderot when Hamas attacked and her son was serving in the army.
One of his friends and fellow soldier, Daniel Peretz, was taken hostage and killed.
She said the destruction in Gaza was "not enough" given the horrors inflicted by Hamas on October 7 and the treatment of Israeli hostages.
Ms Oberman claimed the international community was "distorting" Israel's conduct in Gaza.
"They've taken something that has happened to us, misconstrued it and turned it against us," she said.
Ms Oberman added there has been an increase in antisemitism and an "unwillingness to see that there is no genocide".
A United Nations independent commission has twice found there is sufficient evidence to say Israel was committing a genocide in Gaza.
While other organisations have levelled similar charges, the Netanyahu government has rejected the findings as politically motivated inquiries serving to prop up Hamas.
Israeli voters weigh in on Netanyahu leadership
It is hard to separate the timing of the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks from Israel's national election.
This election will effectively be a referendum on the prime minister, his leadership and insistence he is the only man to keep Israel safe.
Ms Oberman is suspicious of the timing of the reports Mr Netanyahu was forewarned of the attacks.
"If they'd come out with it in November three years ago, I would have said, OK, maybe there's something to it," she said.
She planned to vote for Bezalel Smotrich, the current finance minister in Mr Netanyahu's coalition government and leader of the Religious Zionist Party.
He has been condemned around the world and is subject to sanctions from a number of countries, including Australia, for his inflammatory rhetoric and policies towards Palestinians.
At the Sderot lookout, tour guide Avraham Tuval said he did not support Mr Netanyahu before the war began and ultimately holds the government responsible.
"The government was in charge when it happened and they have full responsibility for everything that happened that day and since then 'til today," he said.
Demands for accountability
Intelligence and planning failures, which not only allowed Hamas to prepare for its deadly assault but left authorities flat-footed when the attacks began, are central issues in this election.

Most of Mr Netanyahu's political opponents are demanding he establish an independent national inquiry, including former Israel Defense Forces chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar Party is recording strong support in the polls.
Mr Netanyahu has rejected the proposal.
Mali Zender's 22-year-old daughter Noa was a victim of the attack on the Nova music festival near the town of Re'im, where 378 people were killed and 44 taken hostage.
Ms Zender and her family are still desperately seeking answers.
"No-one is giving the answers to let us know what happened over there, that can make us crazy," she said.
Ms Zender said it did not matter who replaced Mr Netanyahu's government, but a national inquiry must be held.
"We are a very strong army, a strong country … we have such strong intelligence, how did this happen?"
As head nurse at Tel Aviv's Sheba Hospital, Ms Zender oversaw the treatment of returning hostages from Gaza.
The importance of her job and wanting to see the Israeli captives cared for tempers her own feelings of loss.
"The longing and the pain are unbearable," she said.
"But at the same time, it brought happiness seeing the kids going back to their parents and their family and be reunited."
